title: What price elasticity of demand means

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define price elasticity of demand as the measure of how strongly the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in its own price, and state what the measure is for.

blocks.heading: Responsiveness, measured
blocks.text: Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how strongly the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in its own price. Topic 2.3 established that a lower price tends to bring a larger quantity demanded; PED puts a number on that tendency. Two markets can obey the same law and behave very differently: when fuel prices rise, drivers in Windhoek may cut back little, while a rise in the price of marula juice may empty a stall in Oshakati. Three parts of the definition do the work. It is about the good's own price, so a substitute's price change sits outside the measure. It works with quantities demanded at prices, the relationship topic 2.3 drew as a demand curve. And it measures degree, not a yes or no: every demand curve responds somehow, and PED says how much.

blocks.heading: Not the same measure as supply's
blocks.text: The confusion learners make: price elasticity of demand and price elasticity of supply are mixed up, because both attach to a price change. The boundary: the demand version measures how buyers respond - the change in quantity demanded when the good's own price changes. The supply version, taught in topic 2.8, measures how sellers respond - the change in quantity supplied. The test: ask which side of the market the quantity belongs to. Petrol stations cutting opening hours after a price fall is a supply response; households buying fewer litres is a demand response.

blocks.heading: One question, two answers
blocks.text: Put the definition to work. A bus fare between Katutura and the city centre rises from N$10 to N$12: some commuters walk, and PED will measure how far quantity demanded fell, as a percentage. Household electricity in Swakopmund rises by a similar percentage: few households can light their homes another way, so quantity demanded falls by less. "Demand falls" is the beginning of an answer; how far it falls is the rest. Sellers setting prices and governments setting taxes both need that second number.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: This measure sits on the demand curve drawn in topic 2.3 and feeds the price decisions examined in topic 2.6 and the supply-side elasticity of topic 2.8.
